title: The Complete Guide to Pop-Up Debates
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart lays out his complete method for Pop-Up Debates, one of three core speaking/listening structures he recommends for a classroom. The rules are minimal, every student speaks at least once and students pop up from their seats to speak, but the guide's real substance is the multi-week onramp he uses to build students toward their first debate, plus the three hurdles, public speaking anxiety, speech delivery, and speech content, he coaches students through using tools like PVLEGS and Paraphrase Plus. He also addresses classroom-management wrinkles: side talk, cross talk, video recording for self-feedback, and why disagreement should be actively encouraged rather than avoided.
points: Before ever announcing a Pop-Up Debate, Stuart spends three weeks running daily Think-Pair-Shares so that share mode, speaking to the whole class, already feels normal by the time the first debate happens.

He explicitly normalizes public-speaking nervousness after the first debate by polling students on who felt at least 1% nervous, reliably getting most hands raised, which he frames as proof students belong.
The three hurdles, public speaking anxiety, speech delivery, and speech content, are treated sequentially, with PVLEGS fixing delivery and Paraphrase Plus fixing content and preventing silo speaking.
Stuart reframes disagreement as a sign of respect rather than conflict, telling students that being argued with in a Pop-Up Debate means they were listening and took the speaker's words seriously.
quotes: Every student must speak at least one time. Students may not speak more than twice, unless the teacher indicates otherwise. To speak, students simply stand up (pop up) at their seats.
In the technical and competitive senses, my Pop-Up Debates are not debates. They are argument-laden discussions where students bring evidence, logic, and reasoning to the prompt at hand.

Anxiety around public speaking often makes you feel like you are the only one who's nervous. But the reality is, you're not. We'll keep working on this so you can gain comfort and confidence as the school year progresses.
The absolute best feedback I can provide my students as public speakers is letting them see themselves on video.

I often tell students that the greatest sign of respect you can receive in a Pop-Up Debate is when someone argues with what you've said. This means that they were listening and that they've taken your words seriously.
One of many reasons I love the Pop-Up Debate tool is that it gives my students proof that they Belong in my class.
